full_text:
Last year, 18 players mattered in fantasy football.

I didn’t invent that number out of thin air; it’s the number of players who appeared on a roster that made the playoffs in at least 55% of *ESPN* leagues. I’ve listed them below.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/b38097be42066d3fd5a451d5799cc665602e527a)

In [*Upside Wins Championships*](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2021/upside-wins-championships-redux#/), Scott Barrett dubbed these “power-law players,” before going on to demonstrate that this elite group is measurably responsible for the vast majority of weekly wins and yearly championships.

Replacement-level production (“floor”) is readily available on the waiver wire at most positions in the most popular fantasy football formats. Moreover, the “floor” for your fantasy season — finishing in last place — is identical in outcome to finishing third, or fourth, or wherever the payouts end. __All of this incentivizes us to aim high, to try to find one of those few scarce power-law players with every draft pick we make, to maximize our odds of victory.__

In this piece, I’ve painstakingly broken down every trend and angle we can use to predict ahead of time who these “league-winners” will be in 2026. In analyzing nine seasons of data against current ADP market conditions, I aimed to develop an optimal position-by-position draft strategy based on these principles.

__At the end of it all, I’ve landed on the 18 players going after Round 1 who I believe will ascend to league-winner status__ *__this__* __year.__

\> Note: This is a *long* article. I’ve done all my homework this offseason and shown my work in detail. Feel free to use the section headers throughout and quickly find what interests you; __I__ __won’t be offended if you skip to a particular positional strategy, the player writeups, or__ __the overall TL;DR at the bottom.__

Methodology
-----------

“League winner” is a term often used (and abused) quite loosely. But in this article, it will very strictly refer to the power-law players who __appeared on at least 55% of playoff rosters in__ *__ESPN’s__* __default format.__ I may refer to this as “playoff rate” or “win rate” throughout. This data is sourced from [Tristan Cockroft’s yearly articles](https://www.espn.com/fantasy/football/story/_/id/47181388/fantasy-football-playoffs-most-common-players-2025) on the subject.

Why care about this metric? It provides a look at how players helped or hurt fantasy teams in actual leagues, integrating their average acquisition costs (and opportunity costs) while skipping past any debates about how much a player must “beat ADP” to be regarded as a successful pick. It also has the advantage of drawing on the vast majority of the fantasy season, compared to a metric like “[Championship rate](https://www.espn.com/fantasy/football/story/_/id/47454522/2025-fantasy-football-champions-most-common-players),” which more heavily relies on a smaller sample of playoff performances in Weeks 15-17.

These league-winning players from past seasons can be viewed under each positional section (labeled “League-Winning Quarterbacks,” “Running Backs,” etc.) throughout this article.

##### League Settings

__Importantly, the more closely your league mirrors__ *__ESPN’s__* __default settings__ — *10 teams, with 4 teams making the playoffs, PPR scoring, and with lineups starting 1 QB, 2 RBs, 2 WRs, 1 TE, 1 FLEX, and optionally a K and D/ST* — __the more applicable this article’s findings and analysis will be for you__.

It won’t be too far off if you’re in a 12-team league, but lineup variations like a Superflex spot, additional WR spots, or TE-premium scoring will significantly shift relative positional values from what is discussed here. However, most of the archetypal features of a “league-winning” player we’ll discuss (the indicators we’re looking for *within* positions) should hold up relatively well across formats.

##### Timeframes

Our data on these league-winning players goes back to 2017. Therefore, 2017 through 2025 (nine seasons) will make up our main sample for the bulk of this analysis.

However, you’ll also often see me switch to “since 2021” (the past five seasons), as that’s how far our charted data goes back in the [*Fantasy Points Data Suite*](https://data.fantasypoints.com/). So some of the most powerful stats on which we’ll rely in this piece — like expected fantasy points (XFP) and first downs per route run (1D/RR) — can only be used across this timeframe.

Which Positions Are The Most Important?
---------------------------------------

If you were to ignore any previous knowledge of fantasy football, how would you go about finding the answer to the above question?

I’m not sure there’s any one optimal method, but the several I try below all yield similar results, which makes me more confident in the answer. Let’s begin by checking which positions our “league winners” have played:

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/768e7a1c3661f6a82a2704c1b8d4bb64509af912)

__Comparing these proportions__, __it would follow that RBs are roughly 1.3x as valuable as WRs, who are in turn roughly 2.7x as valuable as QBs and TEs.__ Defenses and kickers bring up the rear, offering roughly one-half and one-fourth the value of QBs/TEs, respectively.

Viewed another way, RBs account for nearly 39% of league-winners, even though they comprise just 25% of your lineup spots (excluding the FLEX) by *ESPN’s* default settings. From that, we could calculate they’re roughly ~1.55x more important than their lineup space would imply. By the same logic, WRs have 1.23x the expected importance, QBs have 0.94x, and TEs have ~0.87x. D/STs and Ks bring up the rear at 0.41x and 0.23x, respectively. This more conservative method implies RBs/WRs are between ~1.3x and ~1.8x more valuable than QBs/TEs rather than ~3.0x, but the takeaway is similar in practice.

A separate *a priori* approach through the lens of positional scarcity — as Adam Harstad explained best [here](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1271493180459016193?s=20) — also gets us in this ballpark.

And finally, we get similar results with the Value Over Replacement Player (VORP) method, which compares the fantasy points per game (FPG) offered by the top-3 starters at each position to those of the bottom-3 starters. (In a 10-team league, we’d consider 10 starting TEs and QBs, and 20 starting RBs and WRs). Over the last 14 seasons, a top RB has again generated approximately 1.3x the value over replacement of a top WR. Here, RBs and WRs are somewhere between 1.4x and 2.2x more valuable than QBs and TEs.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/46aa24da6e043bf8ee484f532b03e4beb0384d21)

What happens if we break this down by season? Not much changes: in each of the past nine individual years, the RB and WR positions have produced more league winners than QB and TE.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/85c298959cd62570fca3b6a434691a7383d8ff47)

__From all of this, we can conclude that RBs and WRs are somewhere between 1.3x and 3.0x more valuable than all other positions, with RBs narrowly winning out between the two. QBs and TEs are roughly as valuable as each other, while K and D/ST values are negligible compared to everything else.__

When Should You Draft Each Position?
------------------------------------

Below, I’ve charted the percentage of players since 2017 who became a league winner among all players drafted at the same position and within the same round (by *ESPN* ADP, assuming a 10-team league). For example, 22% of RBs drafted in Round 1 became league winners, compared to 7% of RBs drafted in Round 13 doing the same.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/9ab45fa33ebd27ef16886c3d80a1900a4031975b)

Your immediate reaction to the above numbers might be to conclude that you’ve had a much better chance of drafting a league-winner at TE (43%) than at any other position in Round 2, and that you should therefore target a TE there in 2026. You might come to a similar conclusion about QBs in Round 3 (38%) or Round 4 (30%). __But you should not use the chart this way; this line of logic overlooks two critical factors.__

One is that there’s __nowhere near a large enough sample__ to draw any conclusions about how good ADP is at identifying upside for an individual position within a single round. That 43% number for Round 2 TEs is actually just “three of seven.” The 38% among Round 3 QBs is actually “five of 13.” And this is to say nothing of the fact that Travis Kelce alone accounts for four of the five league-winning TE seasons we’ve ever had in the first three rounds, while Josh Allen claims four of the five league-winning QB seasons from that range.

In short, we can’t generalize an individual cell to how we should expect the 2026 ADP market to perform. I fell into this trap last year, and regretted it dearly (a season ago, WRs looked slightly better than RBs on this table in the first two rounds, and I overindexed on it *hard*).

The second factor is __opportunity cost__. If you’re drafting a TE or a QB in the first ~four rounds, you’re foregoing one of your only chances to draft a league-winning RB or WR.

That’s a problem for a couple of reasons. Most importantly, league-winners at RB and WR become *significantly* rarer in the late rounds. To illustrate, here’s the share of league-winners each position claims *only in Round 10 and beyond*; suddenly, there are almost no league-winning WRs, and it’s just as easy to find TEs as RBs. QBs are ~50% more represented than they were among the overall league-winner pool.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/0c98681a0037f4c5c51799a61e2aee947ad225c9)

Furthermore, RBs and WRs simply “hit bigger” than QBs and TEs. Taking 2025 as an example, Jonathan Taylor’s 72.3% playoff rate from his Round 2 ADP was *__higher than any TE in the history of our sample__*, and significantly higher than Trey McBride’s from the same season (63.3%). Jaxon Smith-Njigba’s 71.0% in 2025 was also higher than any QB ever (well ahead of Lamar Jackson’s 64.3% win rate in 2024).

The *biggest* hits in the early rounds overwhelmingly happen at RB and WR; just one QB and TE each crack our top-15 by win rate.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/0f2eb627125aa4ff86054e9dd76f1568e131b953)

So even if there’s a (shaky, small sample-reliant) argument that an individual early QB or TE is “safer” (in that their position has previously been more likely to post a strong playoff rate than a random RB or WR), the best early-round outcomes occur at the higher-value RB and WR positions. And remember that we made the same point earlier with VORP; top RBs (+8.9 FPG) and WRs (+7.0) outperform the replacement-level starters at their positions by much more than QBs (+4.1) and TEs (+5.0).

So now that I’ve told you all the ways I wouldn’t use the original chart, let’s examine it again so I can tell you the important takeaways I *am* gleaning from a broader reading.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/9ab45fa33ebd27ef16886c3d80a1900a4031975b)

__1\. In order, the positions at which you’ve had the best chance to find league-winners in the late rounds (10+) are TE, then QB, then RB, then WR.__ Keep this in mind when deciding how to spend your early-round picks, as clicking TEs and QBs is generally the best thing you can be doing late. Clicking late WRs is the worst thing you can be doing.

__2\. At the highest-value positions (RB and WR), you’ve had the best chance within the first two rounds, with the odds gradually decreasing from there.__ If you squint, it’s a relatively uniform drop-off. With each round that passes, you should assume your odds of finding league-winning RBs and WRs grow permanently worse.

__3\. The initial league-winner “window” remains open for longer at WR (through ~Round 9) than at RB (through ~Round 6).__ On average, you’ll have more success pushing off WR selections than RB selections into the middle rounds.

__4\. Drafting a D/ST or K before the final round does not meaningfully increase your odds of finding a league-winner at either position.__ The D/STs and Ks that the market pulls up into earlier rounds don’t pay off any more often than the latest ones.

While our 2026-specific player takes will ultimately inform the positions we draft in each round, these rules provide a general scaffold to keep in mind as we build our draft strategy. If we stray from the above, we had better have particularly good reasons for doing so.

With all that covered, let’s turn our attention to actually identifying league-winning players at each position.

League-Winning Quarterbacks
---------------------------

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/c06b80d17178c22de46ff564e0872f25451e3218)

##### League-Winning QBs Are Usually Hyper-Mobile

Don’t underestimate [Rich Hribar’s](https://x.com/LordReebs?lang=en) “Konami Code;” *every single one* of the league-winning QBs above totaled at least 55 rush attempts in the indicated season. A reasonable rushing workload should be a prerequisite for us to even consider drafting a QB.

{{PAYWALL}}

Since 2021, all 19 QBs to hit 100+ rush attempts have averaged at least 18.5 FPG (roughly the output of a fantasy QB1). Over the same span, 8 of the 10 league-winning QBs above (80%) crested 100 rush attempts.

The most recent one who didn’t — 2025 Patrick Mahomes — averaged 4.3 FPG on scrambles alone (the 3rd-most of any QB in the *Fantasy Points Data* era). __And even with Mahomes included, 9 out of 10 league-winning QB seasons since 2021 (90%) featured 5.0+ total rushing FPG.__

Luckily for us, QB rushing is [among the most stable and predictive](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/fantasy-football-qb-stats-what-matters#/) things in fantasy football from season to season, making our job pretty simple; we can instantly identify league-winning QB candidates based on last year’s rushing volume and production.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/6628948b028b614fcba5e9d375c2f149adcad395)

Evaluating the above data based on the thresholds we outlined, five QBs with meaningful ADPs — __Jordan Love__, __Jared Goff__, __Dak Prescott__, __Joe Burrow__, and __Matthew Stafford__ — paced for fewer than 55 rush attempts. We can virtually eliminate them from true league-winning contention, and the latter three all residing inside the top-nine QBs by *ESPN* ADP appears especially inefficient.

Five QBs — __Jayden Daniels__, __Josh Allen__, __Jalen Hurts__, __Jaxson Dart__, and __Drake Maye__ — were on pace for 100+ rush attempts, suggesting they’re strong bets for a QB1 finish. They’re all (rightfully) being drafted as top-8 QBs on most platforms, but __Kyler Murray__ (who was on pace for nearly 99 rush attempts) and __Malik Willis__ (94, despite not even starting 3 of the 4 games he appeared in) go much later despite barely missing our threshold.

And finally, only seven QBs averaged 5.0 or more rushing FPG last year: Allen, Dart, Willis, Daniels, Hurts, __Trevor Lawrence__, and __Patrick Mahomes__. I’m not that interested in betting on Mahomes to repeat last year’s high-end scrambling performance coming off an ACL/LCL tear (and after [he himself said](https://x.com/goldmctNFL/status/2080748420231225452?s=20) he ran too much!), but Lawrence is intriguing, as we’ll cover below.

##### League-Winning Late-Round QBs Are Usually From One Particular Offensive System

Although no QB drafted in Round 10 or later has hit our 55% playoff rate threshold since 2021 (around the time the ADP market fully understood the value of rushing at the QB position, and began pricing up all the best hyper-mobile QBs out of the late-round range), relaxing it down to 45% to analyze what’s worked in the late rounds seems worthwhile.

Here, we find another glaring trend: the vast majority of successful late-round QBs have had a playcaller from the Kyle Shanahan or Sean McVay (“McShanahan”) coaching tree.

 There are still exactly two paths to success in drafting a QB after Round 10: - Have 100+ rush attempts (Daniels, Maye, Fields) - Play for a "McShanahan" tree playcaller Every late-round QB to make the playoffs in 45%+ of ESPN leagues since 2021 fits one of these two criteria. pic.twitter.com/l7p9gU8oHZ — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 2, 2026 

We get a similar list if we switch to “FPG over ADP-based expectation” as our metric; [six of the top nine](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2015834333660250120?s=20) late-round QBs since 2021 played for a McShanahan tree coach. Over the past two seasons, 22.2% of all McShanahan QBs to be drafted have hit 5.0 or more FPG over expectation, compared to just 6.5% of drafted non-McShanahan QBs. It’s been an effective strategy to just blindly draft a McShanahan QB in the late rounds and log out.

The best explanation I’ve ever mustered for \*why\* these offenses consistently pump out league-best efficiency and strong fantasy outcomes is contained within the intro of [this piece](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/fantasy-football-impact-new-coaches#/) (TL;DR, this coaching tree has been at the forefront of the league in implementing playcalling cheat codes like motion, play action, and heavy personnel). And in [this year’s version](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/new-playcallers-fantasy-football-impact#/) of that piece, I sort through the particulars of every new McShanahan playcaller and my expectations for their players in fantasy (they now control an absurd 44% of the league’s offenses, so it’s more important than ever to look under the hood and choose the right ones!).

I’ll tell you which McShanahan QBs I’m targeting in the player blurbs below, but for completion’s sake, I’d consider __Brock Purdy__, __Matthew Stafford__, __Jordan Love__, __Kyler Murray__, __Malik Willis__, __C.J. Stroud__, __Trevor Lawrence__, __Joe Burrow__, __Jacoby Brissett__, __Justin Herbert__, __Fernando Mendoza__, __Sam Darnold__, __Baker Mayfield__, and __Jalen Hurts__ to have a McShanahan tree playcaller this year.

Quarterback Strategy
--------------------

All the data we’ve reviewed so far in this piece points to two potential strategies at the QB position. They’re the same two we highlighted [last year](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2025/anatomy-of-a-league-winner), but I’m now much more resolute in which one I prefer.

__1) Draft a hyper-mobile QB relatively early (roughly, in Rounds 3-7).__ 90% of all league-winning (55%+ playoff rate) QBs since 2021 fit this description — they were drafted in Round 7 at the latest, and averaged at least 5.0 FPG from rushing. __And in terms of hit rate, this is one of the safest bets you can make in a fantasy draft;__ 10 of 59 (17%) of QBs drafted in Rounds 3-7 have become league-winners, compared to 11% of RBs, 7% of WRs, and 9% of TEs from the same ADP range.

__2) Forego the QB position entirely in the early rounds (until Round 10+),__ accepting that while you may not hit a true league-winner here (the last late-round QB to hit a 55% playoff rate came all the way back in 2020, before the public was as privy to the benefits of rushing), it *has* been extremely easy to find a fantasy QB1 or a “moderate win” at this minimal cost by applying the two criteria (rushing ability and offensive scheme) we discussed above.

*I’m pretty firmly in the second camp this year*, as I’m fully willing to accept 80-90% of the benefit of a Josh Allen if it means I get to preserve my Round 3 pick for a WR or RB. As we’ve touched on, QBs do not have nearly as high a “win rate ceiling” (no QB has ever cracked a 70% win rate, compared to 11 RB/WRs who’ve done so), and top RBs and WRs generate roughly 2x the Value Over Replacement of top QBs. So the opportunity cost — losing an early shot at RB or WR — weighs heavily in my mind, as you’re much less likely to find useful players at those positions in the late rounds.

I’d also argue that much of the reason we haven’t seen a late-round QB hit a 55% win rate recently can be chalked up to variance. There was a wider FPG gap between Allen and a late-round Drake Maye before the fantasy playoffs last year (the period that determines our win rate numbers), but through Week 17, Maye averaged 21.7 FPG to Allen’s 23.6 (meaning Maye finished with about 93% of Allen’s output). If the fantasy regular season were 17 weeks long, Maye (who I called my “absolute favorite QB at cost” in [last year’s version of this article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2025/anatomy-of-a-league-winner)) almost certainly would have hit 55%. Case in point: Maye was on 18% of *championship-winning* rosters last year, the most of any QB.

We can say similar things of both Baker Mayfield (22.6 FPG through 17 weeks, 95% of Allen) and Jayden Daniels (22.5 FPG) as late-round QBs in 2024, who narrowed their regular-season gaps to the top scorers with elite fantasy playoff performances (30.9 and 29.0 FPG, respectively). So I wouldn’t be so sure that the late rounds no longer carry league-winning QB upside; we’ve been just a couple of percentage points of ownership (or a couple of games) away in each of the last two years.

__So, my overall recommendation is to draft a QB in the late rounds.__ If you choose to ignore that advice, you’d have the best reasons for doing so if:

1) Your league is shallow; at least as shallow as an *ESPN* standard league (10 teams, starts only 2 WRs and 1 FLEX).

And…

2) You believe your level of competition to be incredibly soft, and that it’s unlikely any other manager in your league will build a roster with multiple league-winning players if you take one of the “easy” bets (an early QB) off the board.

As more lineup spots and teams get added to your league (meaning RB and WR production get harder to come by), or as you face more competent opponents capable of drafting the correct players at the trickier and higher-value positions (RB and WR), wasting a bullet on an early QB becomes less and less appealing. I already don’t think it’s worth it in most home leagues this year, but if you play in anything more competitive, I *definitely* don’t think it’s worth it.

So it shouldn’t be a surprise that most of the QBs I’m recommending below are of the late(ish)-round variety, and that the one earlier pick I’m suggesting is one with a long track record of league-winning performances who now occasionally falls into a slightly later pick range I’m more comfortable with.

Quarterbacks To Draft Who Could Become League Winners
-----------------------------------------------------

At each position, I’ll highlight a handful of the players I believe best fit the league-winning search criteria and positional draft strategy we discussed above. But my list won’t be fully exhaustive in either sense.

__These lists are in rough order of ADP, and will not include every player I’m targeting, especially as player cost varies by draft platform. Players will simply be listed alongside their most attractive ADP between__ *__ESPN__*__,__ *__Yahoo!__*__, and__ *__Sleeper__*__.__ __These are not my rankings.__ For all of that information, check out my Must-Draft Players piece (which should release shortly after this article, and will be linked here and on my [Twitter account](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath) once it does).

##### __Jalen Hurts__, QB, Philadelphia Eagles (*Sleeper ADP: 67.2, QB6*)

Hurts finished as a league-winner in 2022, 2023, and 2024, or each of the past four seasons outside of last year. Then, in 2025, he averaged 19.3 FPG (~QB7) and is now being drafted right around there as the QB5-QB7 across most platforms after the loss of A.J. Brown. But I think the market has been too quick to punish him. [1] 

Hurts did see a decline from his 2024 rush attempts per game (from 10.0 to 6.6, though that was still the same as Josh Allen) and in his rushing touchdown total (from 14 to 8, the fewest he’s scored since his rookie season), but his rushing role is still elite among QBs. __Hurts led the position__ [2] __in designed rush attempts per game (4.1) and designed rushing XFP/G (3.3).__

And I’m here to submit to you that Hurts and the Eagles did not get meaningfully worse at the “Tush Push” between 2024 and 2025. Hurts’ TD rates on designed attempts inside the 2-yard line (61.1% and 62.5%, respectively) were virtually identical. __The Eagles simply got into scoring position much less often relative to every other season of Hurts’ career (below).__ That’s what largely explains Hurts’ decline in rushing TDs (by far the most important component of his fantasy scoring) to me.

So in my view, all we really need for Hurts to return to his previous status as a top-2 fantasy QB and perennial league-winner is for the Eagles’ offense to bounce back as a whole. On this front, new “[evil genius](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2065150538136567936?s=20)” OC Sean Mannion — who figures to run a [McShanahan-adjacent](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/new-playcallers-fantasy-football-impact#/) offense, introducing more playcalling cheat codes like [under-center dropbacks](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2070634324274106506?s=20), [throws over the middle](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/new-playcallers-fantasy-football-impact#/), and [horizontally breaking routes](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2071717007339278727?s=20) that have helped Hurts’ efficiency in the past — could be just what the doctor ordered. And it would be pretty hard for Mannion to be worse than Kevin Patullo was last year, who dragged the offense to the five-year lows we see above (three other playcallers all fared just fine over this span).

##### __Trevor Lawrence__, QB, Jacksonville Jaguars (*ESPN ADP: 93.3, QB11*)

Lawrence is pretty simple to me. He [ranks 3rd](https://x.com/FantasyPtsData/status/2066591317589934112?s=20) among all QBs in rushing TDs since 2022. He was one of only five QBs to average 5.0 or more rushing FPG across 8+ games last year — a threshold that 90% of league-winners have hit — and he’s by far the cheapest of that group (excluding Patrick Mahomes, who is coming off an ACL tear). __And Lawrence easily led all QBs in FPG (25.8, +3.4 more than anyone else) from Week 12 through the Wild Card round, once Jakobi Meyers and Parker Washington were full-time players in the offense.__

We’ve discussed how later-round QBs with “McShanahan” playcallers tend to overperform; Jaguars HC Liam Coen is perhaps the most QB-friendly McShanahan playcaller there is. __He’s the only one of the group to induce more total QB fantasy production than the coaches who were lucky enough to have superstars like Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow.__ Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay themselves can’t even claim that.

Andy Reid - 20.4 Coen w/ Baker Mayfield and Trevor Lawrence has outdone the guys with Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, Joe Burrow, and Patrick Mahomes. pic.twitter.com/1BtvKuXPQw — Fantasy Points Data (@FantasyPtsData) June 20, 2026 

These points are tied together; both Lawrence (5.2) and Baker Mayfield (3.2) hit career-highs in rushing FPG the season they played under Coen. The two offenses he’s called rank 2nd in fantasy points per dropback (0.53) and 1st in (real) points per game (28.7) among all playcallers over the past five years. I’m not sure why we’re getting such a discount on this Jaguars offense relative to how they performed in the second half of last season, but I’m definitely not complaining.

##### __Justin H____erbert__, QB, Los Angeles Chargers (*ESPN ADP: 107.5, QB15*)

Herbert is an [athletic clone of Josh Allen](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1951018279159419386?s=20). That comparison probably overstates his statistical rushing ceiling, but Herbert still ran the ball much more than you remember last year. He ranked 6th among QBs in rushing YPG (31.1, ahead of Jalen Hurts and Lamar Jackson), 1st in scramble yards (439, ahead of Drake Maye), and tied for 5th in total rush attempts (83, ahead of Caleb Williams).

##### League-Winning RBs Are Drafted Early

62% of the RBs above were drafted within the first four rounds; 70% had an ADP within the first six. The best value pockets to target within those ranges have shifted around over the years, __but it’s always been important and beneficial to draft and hit on RBs in these early and middle rounds.__ We’ll cover the viability of “Zero RB” in the strategy section below.

##### League-Winning RBs Are Usually Young, Especially The First Time

On average, league-winning RBs are 25.1 years old. Furthermore, 85% of our league-winning RBs have been 27 or younger on December 31 of their league-winning season. For all the talk of the position’s shelf life being extended via medical advances, only __Christian McCaffrey__ broke that trend in 2025.

For reference, McCaffrey, __Saquon Barkley__, __Derrick Henry__, and __Josh Jacobs__ will all be 28 or older by the end of the 2026 season. My [*Age Curves*](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/age-curves-when-nfl-players-break-out#/) analysis suggests that elite fantasy RBs are at an escalating risk of a production dropoff in every season from age 29 onward, which applies to each of the former three. That’s more of a note on those players’ floors than their league-winning ceilings (it wouldn’t be the first time McCaffrey or Henry personally defied the age curve, and I’m still in on both for that reason), but it still bears mentioning.

From an NFL experience lens, 9% of league-winning RBs were rookies, 19% were sophomores, 21% were in Year 3, and 15% were in Year 4. __In total, 64% (nearly two-thirds) of league-winning RB seasons come from players on their rookie contract____.__

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/eb67e8c9d7937de769451ec7810046e1dd06b87f)

Perhaps more strikingly, every RB to ever become a league-winner with an ADP inside the first six rounds was either 1) in one of their first four seasons in the NFL, or 2) had already reached league-winning status in a previous season. __In other words, we’ve never had a first-time league-winner past Year 4 of their career who was drafted inside the first six rounds.__ So we should only be interested in older RBs if they’ve done it before.

Faithfully applying that trend, __Kenneth Walker__, __Breece Hall__, __Javonte Williams__, and __David Montgomery__ are all past Year 4, have no prior league-winning seasons to their name, and are drafted inside the first 60 picks on at least one major platform. [3] __In contrast, that same warning was true for only one top-20 RB by ADP in 2025.__ (Chuba Hubbard, who lost his job to Rico Dowdle and gave us just the second undrafted league-winner over the past four seasons.)

Make a mental note of that, as it’s one piece of evidence for the return of the “RB Dead Zone” in 2026. For the first time over the past few years, drafters have returned to placing a premium on projected volume for older backs who’ve yet to offer a truly elite fantasy ceiling over a full season. We’ll further break down what that means for you in the strategy section below.

##### League-Winning RBs Are Either *Elite* Pass-Catchers, Or Barely Catch Any Passes (And Are Being Underdrafted Because Of It)

In planning our early-round picks, it may be beneficial to look closer at the top-20 RBs by win rate from within the first six rounds of ADP (all above a 60% win rate, the best of the best). What do you notice about these players’ archetypes?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/64f76e4a5a189e44ee819be2add246f07de8e74f)

The list is full of “PPR cheat code”-type backs for whom much of their scoring came through the air — Christian McCaffrey, De’Von Achane, Jahmyr Gibbs, Bijan Robinson, Alvin Kamara, and Austin Ekeler all come to mind. That makes sense; a target is [worth](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/statistically-significant-weighted-opportunity#/) 2.55x the fantasy points of a carry for an RB in PPR leagues.

But increasingly, a second, very different archetype of RB has started to succeed in the early rounds. Jonathan Taylor, Derrick Henry, Nick Chubb, James Cook, and Saquon Barkley (in 2024) all make appearances. None of these players commanded more than 54 targets in their league-winning season (for perspective, the average among top-6 scoring RBs over the past five seasons is 68.4 targets, while the average for our top-20 league-winners is 79.1).

Given that, you might expect a lot of the league-winning RBs to have commanded somewhere around 60-100 targets. __But the opposite is true; the majority of our top-20 by win rate (55%) fall outside that range, either far above or far below “average.”__ It’s a wide distribution with a relatively shallow middle, counter to the “normal distribution” or “[bell curve](https://x.com/FantasyKash/status/2074482190151278627?s=20)” we’re conditioned to expect data to fit. [4] 

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/4789b2da90707aba33eef2b9aa5bd4c435bc4c8e)

So it seems like there’s something to the idea of “outlier” profiles — either those who catch very few passes *or* those who catch a lot — having the best odds of becoming league-winners. So far, we’ve only conducted an *ex post* analysis (backward-looking, analyzing an RB’s targets in the same season they broke fantasy leagues); does the same hold up if we use *previous-season* receiving ability?

It does! To test this, I divided RBs into three buckets: Non-Pass Catchers, Average Bellcows, and Elite Pass Catchers. In an attempt to capture archetype and drafters’ perceptions of each player (what ultimately creates league-winners and “value” against ADP), I created the buckets based on the percentage of *Expected* Fantasy Points (XFP, or total fantasy value-adjusted volume) each RB got from receiving work (as opposed to rushing). Non-Pass Catchers got less than 30% of their XFP from receiving, Average Bellcows were between 30 and 40%, and Elite Pass Catchers got over 40%. [5] 

The next step is a bit complicated, but bear with me. By plotting every RB over each of the past five seasons by their ADP and their fantasy points per game result, we can build an “ADP Expectation” curve: the number of FPG we’d expect an RB to average, given their ADP.

For example, RBs drafted at the 10th overall pick are expected to average 16.7 FPG; those drafted at the 80th overall pick are expected to average 9.4 FPG. This gives us a baseline against which to compare each RB’s *actual* FPG result, indicating *by how much* they exceeded or underperformed their cost.

__Exceeding ADP expectation by 5.0 or more points is roughly analogous to a “league-winner” as we’ve discussed them throughout this article__; it just gives slightly more credit to “value picks” at later ADPs who may have been “crowded out” from a high playoff rate by higher-scoring early-round picks in their particular season, but could have been league-winners in another (Bucky Irving and Chase Brown in 2024 [come to mind](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/fantasy-football-takeaways#/)). It also expands our sample to include players who may have played only 10 games (I used an 8-game minimum for the analysis below), or who scored especially well during the fantasy playoff weeks (where our *ESPN* playoff rate cuts off). I thought all this was important to re-expand our sample somewhat after cutting it to only 2022 and on (so that I could use XFP).

So, I checked how often the RBs from each of our three buckets averaged 5.0 or more FPG *above* their ADP-based expectation in the *following* season (year N+1).

__From anywhere within the top-100 picks, “Non-Pass Catchers” and “Elite Pass Catchers” have vastly exceeded their ADP expectation at much higher rates than the “Average Bellcows” in the middle of the spectrum.__ This aligns with our target-total-based observation of early-round league-winning RBs from earlier.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/dc7b7385ae34fc55f91fb7fe05921bd12e82f6c9)

For years, I (and many other analysts) have preached that pass-catching is the most desirable trait for a fantasy football RB. So what's going on here? Why do non-pass catchers perform so well against ADP, and why do the average-but-not-elite pass-catchers perform so poorly?

I think this is mostly about market dynamics, and how drafters categorically penalize and avoid “non-pass catchers” to a suboptimal degree. Let me explain.

Below is every non-pass catcher with a top-100 ADP since 2022, sorted in ADP order. What do you notice?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/9da0af1b2163dd48ce20b1202b0eab4416b12cf9)

Non-pass catchers have indeed been *awful* bets inside the first ~18.0 picks, containing two of the bigger busts in recent memory (2022 Jonathan Taylor and 2025 Saquon Barkley) and not a single RB to exceed expectation by even 2.0 points (for perspective, 31% of elite pass-catchers did so from inside the first 18 picks). __It’s been when players like Taylor, Henry, and Cook get pushed into the end of Round 2 or later that they’ve had room to dramatically overperform that ADP and become league-winners.__

Just as critically, the “non-pass catcher” RB is [extremely gamescript-sensitive](https://x.com/FantasyPts/status/2066491095593185483?s=20); that is, they perform much better in fantasy when their teams are winning than when they’re losing. If the Ravens are trailing, Derrick Henry often isn’t even on the field. Jonathan Taylor averages only 13.8 FPG in losses over the past five seasons. The more passes an RB catches, the [safer their floor](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2062969643279802517?s=20) (the less likely they are to dramatically *under*perform ADP, due to being game-scripted out thanks to a bad defense or a QB injury).

So it shouldn’t be surprising that all our 5.0+ FPG overperformers above were on teams that won at least 8 games. And some of the middle-round success stories (Rhamondre Stevenson, Isiah Pacheco, and Kenneth Walker) simply grew as pass-catchers in Year 2 or Year 3, setting career-high per-game target and reception averages in a year that ADP still treated them as two-down players.

To tie all this information up into a neat set of rules, here are the types of RBs I’ll be targeting for their league-winning ceilings, regarding archetype:

1\. __Elite pass-catchers are high-ceiling, high-floor picks regardless of ADP.__ Using our XFP-from-receiving-based cutoff from above, __Christian McCaffrey__, __Bijan Robinson__, __Jahmyr Gibbs__, __De’Von Achane__, __Ashton Jeanty__, __Chase Brown__, and __Omarion Hampton__ all saw over 40% of their XFP from receiving last year. Some notable middle-round names from this category include __Rachaad White__, __RJ Harvey__, and __Aaron Jones__.

2\. __Non-pass catchers have lower floors (more ways to bust if their offenses let them down), but they frequently hit league-winning ceilings if at least two of the following apply:__

+ They’re drafted outside the top-18 picks — or, more broadly, you’re getting a discount just for the fact that they don’t catch passes.

+ Their team is good enough to provide frequent positive gamescript (8+ wins at minimum, and preferably more)
+ ADP (or, broadly, public perception) is simply wrong about how many passes they’ll catch, which happens most frequently for younger backs.

Notable RBs who accumulated less than 30% of their XFP from receiving last year — and therefore fit into this non-pass catcher bucket — include __Jonathan Taylor, James Cook, Kenneth Walker, Derrick Henry, Quinshon Judkins, David Montgomery, Bhayshul Tuten,__ and __J.K. Dobbins__. Taylor and Cook go in Round 1 (meaning that ADP is taking for granted that their teams’ seasons will go perfectly, and making them inherently risky with only arguably better upside than players like Walker and Henry, in my view), but the rest are names to be considered against points 2b and 2c.

##### The “Running Back Dead Zone” Is Back

Last year [in this space](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2025/anatomy-of-a-league-winner#/), I told you not to be afraid of drafting RBs in the “Running Back Dead Zone” — classically said to span roughly from Rounds 4 through 6 — so long as they had strong receiving and talent-based profiles.

For a while, those rounds of drafts were descriptively a “dead zone”; __they produced just 0.6 league-winning RBs per season from 2017 to 2021.__ But as fantasy drafters became aware of that trend and got choosier about the RB profiles they’d draft in that range (focusing on talent, youth, and receiving upside over projectable volume for average-at-best players), the trend changed; __Rounds 4-6 averaged 1.8 league-winning RBs from 2022-2025__, with James Cook joining the list last year.

From that story, we can extract a lesson: the “RB Dead Zone” is not a literal group of rounds, but a phenomenon born from perceived scarcity. When drafters feel pressure to fill their RB spots and begin selecting weaker, lower-upside RB profiles ahead of more deserving players at other positions, a “dead zone” is created.

Just from observing the number of RBs being drafted in the early rounds, we can infer that this wasn’t really happening over the previous three seasons (when the former “dead zone” was actually seeing success). But we’re now right back to the same number of RBs being selected through four rounds on *ESPN* as we saw back in 2017, and we’re [nearly there](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2077899750616027310?s=20) by FantasyData ADP (an aggregate of several sources) as well.

__A low supply of high-end bellcow backs meets a high demand, driving up the price of even the mediocre imitations.__

But who are the mediocre imitations that we should avoid? If we circle back to our “average bellcows” from the section above — RBs who saw between 30% and 40% of their XFP from receiving, who aren’t elite pass-catchers but also aren’t penalized within the psychology of the drafting public for “not catching passes” — then I think we’ve found our “dead zone” backs.

These players are legitimately “[safer](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2062969643279802517?s=20)” than non-pass catchers. __But they hit league-winning ceilings at much lower rates, precisely because of the ADP premium you’re paying for that perceived safety.__

Roughly in order of ADP, the RBs in the top six rounds who fall into this bucket based on their 2025 usage are __Saquon Barkley__, __Josh Jacobs__, __Breece Hall__, __Travis Etienne, Javonte Williams, Bucky Irving, Cam Skattebo, TreVeyon Henderson,__ and __D’Andre Swift__. __Kyren Williams__ (29.0%) is just under the cutoff, but I’m choosing to count him for the reason I’m about to explain.

I’m explicitly *not* telling you to cross all of those names off your draft board. Just as the dead zone is not a magical group of rounds to avoid, it’s also not a magical group of “% of XFP gained from receiving last year” to avoid. It’s more of a tool to gain insight into drafters’ psychology: __which of the RBs I just mentioned above are seen as “safe” options who will catch a decent number of passes, which a skittish manager might select to stabilize the RB1 or RB2 spot in their lineup without regard for upside?__

That’s an inherently subjective question, but I have pretty strong feelings on it. (Don’t worry, I’m going to back up my fades with tangibly researched player takes.)

Barkley and Jacobs aren’t necessarily my favorite picks on the board, but they’ve both been league-winners before in similar or worse offensive environments, so I’m not about to dismiss them as “dead zone” backs out of hand.

I also don’t think anybody drafting Skattebo, Henderson, or Swift is under any illusions that they’re riskless and stable picks who can be expected to garner every backfield touch. They’re gambling on the high-end upside outcome if they rid themselves of the backfield competition that limited them last year (in Henderson’s and Swift’s cases), or if they can repeat previously demonstrated high-end upside upon [returning from injury](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2056752913913991666?s=20) in a [projected bad offense](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/new-playcallers-fantasy-football-impact#/) (in Skattebo’s case). I’d have included Irving in the next group rather than this one had I written this article on May 1, but he has fallen in ADP (in my view, correctly) all summer due to similar role uncertainty.

For the rest — Hall, Etienne, and both Williamses (Javonte and Kyren) — I think they’re drafted where they are *precisely* because managers are kidding themselves about their outlooks and stability as the engines of their respective offenses.

Hall *is* an [amazing receiver](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2064418269981741226?s=20) and would make our “Elite Pass Catcher” category in a just world, but that’s not the world we live in; Aaron Glenn is [going to make sure of that](https://x.com/ZackBlatt/status/2064732016088629376?s=20). A significant portion of the fantasy football community suffers from Kyren Williams Derangement Syndrome. I understand that some people were annoying and wrong about Blake Corum “stealing his job” immediately after he was drafted, but that doesn’t mean we should ignore the [very real cap](https://x.com/KyleM_FF/status/2081559097623871516?s=20) Corum now places on Williams’ upside. Last year, Williams fell to just a 60.0% designed carry share (~RB19) after ranking top-5 at the position in that metric over each of the previous two seasons. The Rams’ offense still hummed — ranking top-5 in rush attempts from inside the 10-yard line (53) — with Williams still scoring double-digit rushing TDs. So if not that, what could improve for Williams that would allow him to break past the borderline RB1 range? That’s really my hang-up with all of these “dead zone” backs — how could anything get better to propel them past the low-end RB1 range and into true league-winning status? That’s my bar for any ~top-40 pick.

As I’ve demonstrated, none can be counted on for an elite receiving role (and only Hall has *ever* really had one), so — much like the non-pass catcher group we discussed earlier — their paths to league-winning upside rely on rushing TDs or big plays. __Etienne and both of the Williamses were in strong offenses__ *__last year__*__; all of them ranked top-8 in carries inside the 10-yard line (ahead of players like James Cook) yet failed to average more than 15.6 FPG____.__

And none of these backs are great bets (relative to later-drafted ones) to generate big plays on their own, either; D’Andre Swift (the RB24 on *ESPN*) demolished them all in explosive run rate last year (15.1%, 5th-best). This isn’t me suffering from “dynasty brain.”

I’m not even saying you can’t hunt for touchdowns with stable veterans on good teams; I’d just prefer you do it later in your draft. All of these dead zone backs go 1-3 rounds earlier than Montgomery, Judkins, Swift, Tuten, and Rhamondre Stevenson, despite (at most) a ~1.0-2.0 point gap in median [projection](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/projections/season/rb-wr#/). Whatever your favorite flavor of bet is from that fivesome, I’d much rather you draft them at ADP than one of the four from the dead zone.

##### Handling Late Round RBs

In the middle and later rounds, league-winning RB hit rates have been generally higher than at WR, but generally lower than at QB and TE. However, you have several late-round picks to use, with only two (at most) being earmarked for QB and TE, so it makes sense to take later shots at the RB position regardless of your early draft strategy.

Keep in mind that these later RB picks will be prime drop candidates for early-season waiver wire pickups, so it behooves you to select RBs on whom we’ll gain information in Week 1. Short of an injury occurring exactly within the first four quarters of football, there’s little opportunity for pure handcuffs like __Tank Bigsby__ or __Isiah Pacheco__ to gain value and convince you not to drop them.

The same isn’t true for players in more ambiguous backfields like __Rachaad White__/__Jacory Croskey-Merritt__, __Jonathon Brooks__, __J.K. Dobbins__/__RJ Harvey__, __Kenny Gainwell__, __Jaylen Warren__/__Rico Dowdle__, __Aaron Jones__/__Jordan Mason__, __Blake Corum__, or __Chris Rodriguez__. Even if many of these are low-percentage bets to ultimately matter, you’re simply buying the chance to see their Week 1 snap shares. Occasionally, you’ll stumble into a 51.9% Week 1 share for a player like Gainwell in 2025, which might have convinced you to hold onto him long enough to benefit from the 17.8 FPG he averaged over the final eight weeks.

##### Can You Go “Zero RB” And Add League-Winning RBs Off The Waiver Wire?

The short answer is “no.” I don’t think it’s that simple.

Across nine seasons, we’ve seen just 11 league-winning RBs who went undrafted (comprising only 21% of all league-winners at the position). That’s an average of just over one chance to add a league-winning RB per season.

And as preseason news coverage and most sites’ default rankings have improved over the past four seasons, it’s been even more dire; only 2 league-winning UDFA RBs have emerged since 2022 (0.5 per season).

If you assume there are nine other active managers in your league playing the waiver wire against you, you have just a 1-in-10 chance of being the one to add a particular league-winning UDFA RB. Even if you’re an effective FAAB bidder and half your league is asleep at the wheel, your odds are perhaps 1-in-5 at best. And that’s *on* *top* of the uncertain chance that a UDFA league-winner emerges at all this season. __In contrast, 21.7% of RBs drafted in Rounds 1-4 have become league-winners; those are much better odds!__

A properly-executed “Zero RB” team requires you to add several ambiguous and contingent bets throughout the middle and late rounds of your draft, in hopes that enough of them hit for your advantage at all other positions to keep you afloat. So let’s consider the strongest version of the Zero RB thesis, rather than the strawman.

In contrast to the past two seasons having blessed us with immaculate RB health, if you draft a Zero-RB team, the bet you’re *truly* making is that the above trend reverts to the longer-term pattern; that significantly more RBs get injured than WRs. That would both help WRs outperform RBs in the early rounds *and* ensure the contingent RB bets (other managers’ handcuffs you draft late) pay off.

As 2015 showed us, such an outcome can happen in any season, no matter how well the RBs scored the year before. And considering that ADP has finally shifted back to its pre-2023 norms with more RBs going early (as we covered above), 2026 is probably the best out of any recent season in which to go Zero RB. You’d actually be zigging while others zag.

Don’t get it twisted, though; all the data we’ve reviewed throughout this article mostly points to RBs possessing higher ceilings than WRs in the early rounds. RBs have made up the largest share of the overall pool of league-winners in most past seasons, and selecting RBs early has proved a winning strategy more often than it hasn’t.

Zero-RB is best applied as a part of a portfolio of teams in case injury variance comes in and throws a wrench in all our analysis in a given year; it’s more of a bet on what we don’t know than on what we do, and it therefore shouldn’t be your strategy if you’re only drafting a single team. [6] 

I say all this because I did “get it twisted” last year; though I stopped short of full-on recommending Zero-RB, I did tell you to lean toward WRs in early rounds based on what were, in hindsight, too-small samples (read last year’s version of [*Anatomy*](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2025/anatomy-of-a-league-winner#/) and note how often I relied on only the previous three years to make a WR-related point). Many of the trends I’d identified — like Round 1 WRs having better win rates than RBs from 2022 on, or their ADP-to-FPG correlations looking better than RBs in early rounds over a similarly brief sample — partially or completely reversed with just one more season of data. And considering that RBs were so dominant in most pre-2021 seasons, maybe that was all just a relic of the most pass-heavy version of the NFL we'd ever seen, which no longer exists.

To conclude, the reason to go Zero-RB in 2026 *should not* be because you think you’ve peered into the matrix and discovered that WRs are secretly better bets than RBs in a vacuum. You can also [count me as a skeptic](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2079643462111289404?s=20) that the league-wide shift to multi-TE sets is a reason to believe Zero RB will succeed this year (though that trend will have implications for our WR strategy, as we’ll discuss further down).

Zero RB is instead a way to exploit the industry’s return to drafting more RBs early, and you should only expect it to work if 1) injuries strike or 2) several contingent/ambiguous backfield bets in the late rounds pay off.

But in the context of a single 10- or 12-team managed redraft league, just avoiding the newly returned RB dead zone (described above) and drafting a few strong late-round RB bets *in addition* to any you take early should still give you a great chance to win in that worst-case scenario.

##### Putting It All Together (RB Strategy TL;DR)

So, we want to avoid the new RB dead zone, which in my view begins at about the RB15 (once Chase Brown, Kenneth Walker, and Josh Jacobs are off the board), or by the mid-3rd round.

We’ll also want to draft several of the best WR values I’m going to outline later in this article. No spoilers, but I see a ton of value among middle-round WRs this year.

Finally, given that we don’t want to draft a Zero RB team, it makes a lot of sense to get our RBs in Rounds 1 and 2, where they just happen to have posted their best historical league-winner rates.

Based on the default ADP for *ESPN*, *Yahoo!*, and *Sleeper*, I see no reason why I wouldn’t leave the first two rounds of every draft with *at least* one RB, if not two of them.

##### League-Winning WRs Are Already Amazing By First Downs Per Route Run

For those unfamiliar, [first downs per route run](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/statistically-significant-first-downs-per-rr#/) (1D/RR) is an efficiency stat similar to the more popular yards per route run (YPRR), with the critical difference that 1D/RR rewards consistent chain-moving WRs over inconsistent, big-play-reliant ones. It’s also the [most predictive efficiency stat](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2065065514045460857?s=20) for WRs in all of fantasy football.

And it’s especially useful for spotting league-winners. Since 2021, the WRs above have averaged 0.129 1D/RR within their league-winning season. __The year prior, those same WRs averaged 0.124 1D/RR — only a 4% difference.__

For comparison, league-winning WRs saw a 10% boost in YPRR, a 17% boost in targets, a 21% boost in receiving yards, or a 32% boost in touchdowns. __1D/RR is one of the only stats in which they didn’t see a large increase, making it perfect for spotting league-winning candidates a season early.__

From 2021 to 2024, 35 different WRs averaged at least 0.116 1D/RR across a minimum of 250 routes. __15 of them (43%!) became league-winners in the following season.__ And 11 of *those* 15 (73%) weren’t drafted in Round 1, suggesting that 1D/RR isn’t fully priced in as an indicator.

##### Avoiding The WR Cliff

There are two ways to conceptualize the “WR Cliff,” and both lead us to the same strategic conclusion.

We already covered the first: __we’ve never seen a league-winning WR drafted after Round 12, and your odds of finding one continually fall from Round 4 onward.__ You get a longer “tail” of upside at WR than at most positions through the middle rounds (6-9), but then the door closes completely. __Only 4.5% of all league-winners from Rounds 10-17 have been WRs.__ So use those shots while you still have them!

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/9ab45fa33ebd27ef16886c3d80a1900a4031975b)

The other way of viewing the WR cliff is through the “total number of useful players,” or “number of players who could theoretically be a WR2/FLEX.”

It might feel like there are an endless number of WRs who can average ~12.0 FPG competing for your FLEX spot, but that’s becoming less true over time.

For reference, 138 of the 163 WRs (85%) to average 12.0 or more FPG since 2021 have run a route on at least 75% of their team’s dropbacks; it’s exceedingly difficult to be a useful fantasy asset if you aren’t on the field at least this much. So to control away touchdown variance, let’s define a “potentially useful” WR as one who commands at least a 75% route share.

__Only 40 WRs cleared that low bar in 2025, meaning there were 25% fewer “potentially useful” WRs than in 2021.__ The number has trended down each season, but last year’s low was no doubt driven at least in part by the decline in the number of offenses that ran most of their pass plays with 3+ WRs on the field.

So even if the NFL’s heavy personnel trends [can’t be blamed for an](https://x.com/ChrisWechtFF/status/2012258210061693260?s=20) [*overall*](https://x.com/ChrisWechtFF/status/2012258210061693260?s=20) decline in WR production, or a decline among the top ~24 (as it [makes them more efficient](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/)), I think we can expect there to be fewer overall fantasy-viable WRs going forward. Just think of it as the floor having fallen out, not the ceiling.

__In short, we should only expect it to become harder to draft both “league-winning” and “usable” WRs in the later rounds. So aim to grab at least 4-5 of them before the cliff hits in Round ~10 or 11__. (This cutoff won’t line up perfectly in practice, but for a rough idea, the WR40 gets selected at pick 107.0 overall on *ESPN*.)

So in concert with the analysis on the “RB Dead Zone” above, I’m pretty motivated to select WRs in Rounds ~3-10 this year.
