##### League-Winning TEs Have Previously Been Heavily Targeted and Highly Involved…

The league-winning TEs above collectively averaged 8.0 targets per game, a mark no TE aside from __Trey McBride__ reached in 2025. None of them — even the very late-round picks and UDFAs — averaged fewer than 6.0 targets per game.

We can similarly judge a TE’s upside by his previous-season targets per game. Excluding Darren Waller (who had not played at TE before his league-winning season) as well as 2018 George Kittle and 2019 Mark Andrews (each of whom was entering their 2nd season in the NFL), these TEs similarly averaged 7.7 targets per game in their previous season, with __none averaging fewer than 5.4.__

Most veteran TEs currently being selected inside the top-20 at the position fulfill or nearly fulfill that criterion, but __Mark Andrews__ (3.9), __T.J. Hockenson__ (4.4), __Brenton Strange__ (4.9), and __Hunter Henry__ (4.9) are the most notable and clear-cut players to miss out, all of whom I’m okay with eliminating.

__Isaiah Likely__ is arguably a different case — as he’s never been in a full-time role for an entire season, which figures to change this year — but even across 10 games above a 70% route share since 2022, he averages just 4.8 targets per game (even if his 12.2 FPG within that split sounds pretty nice at his ADP).

Another angle to consider is pure route volume. The overall fantasy TE1 has led the position in routes run over each of the past five seasons. And the route leader has ranked top-3 in fantasy scoring in every season since 2016. (Shoutout to Rich Hribar and Jacob Gibbs for [these excellent pulls](https://x.com/jagibbs_23/status/2076817718142030028?s=20).)

Since 2021, our group of league-winning TEs averaged 31.3 routes per game. For perspective on how high a bar this is, only McBride and __Brock Bowers__ reached that number in 2025. During __Colston Loveland’s__ late-season stretch from Week 15 on (including playoffs) — when the Bears [shifted their offense](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2053917097202479465?s=20) into one that utilized multiple TEs on half or more of their dropbacks — he was running 30.3 routes per game.

__Sam LaPorta__ (26.8 routes per game in 2023) and __George Kittle__ (25.6 routes per game in 2024) have each recently become league-winners on less route volume, so this isn’t a hard-and-fast rule for middle- and later-round TEs. But our league-winning candidates should have a path to either league-high route volume *or* incredible efficiency.

##### …Unless They Were Entering Year 1 or 2

You can largely throw everything I just said out the window for rookie or sophomore TEs. __Six of the seven league-winners above from Round 10 or later were in their first or second season playing the TE position.__ Furthermore, major volume increases were a part of the league-winning Year 2 breakouts of Mark Andrews and George Kittle.

The Year 2 TE breakout has long been one of fantasy football’s [most potent cheat codes](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/age-curves-when-nfl-players-break-out#/), with that being the season in which ~50% of all elite TEs broke into the top-6 at the position for the first time. And more recently, the rookies have seen success; over the past three seasons, we’ve had three league-winning rookie TEs from the late rounds (Sam LaPorta, Brock Bowers, and Tyler Warren).

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/6c5c63b7f5e7929eafc4d72ca6860368035a91c6)

That said, considering that the top prospects in the 2023-25 [rookie classes](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/scott-barretts-analytics-darlings-tes#/) were miles ahead of the 2026 [rookie class](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/ryan-heaths-rookie-te-rankings#/), it makes the most sense to focus on this year’s sophomores (2025’s rookies). __Colston Loveland__, __Tyler Warren__, and __Harold Fannin__ all go inside the top-6 at the position already, but Year 2 breakout candidates like __Oronde Gadsden__, __Terrance Ferguson__, __Gunnar Helm__, __Elijah Arroyo__, and __Mason Taylor__ have been all but forgotten by ADP.

None of this is to say that older TEs aren’t viable league-winning candidates; 8 of 15 league-winning seasons on our list (53%) occurred in Year 5 or later. But we shouldn’t be as willing to excuse a lack of previous target-earning for these players.

##### League-Winning TEs Usually Aren’t On Crowded Offenses…

Opposite to what we discussed at WR, a crowded passing offense is generally a negative signal at the TE position.

__14 of our 15 league-winners above came from offenses where there were__ *__not__* __multiple other pass-catchers being drafted inside the top-60 by ADP.__ The one exception — 2024 George Kittle — benefitted from Brandon Aiyuk and Deebo Samuel missing a combined 14 games.

This is because TEs typically require substantial target shares to be league winners. And most of the time, when a TE and a WR are competing for targets, the WR is going to win out.

NFL target distributions occur in a “trickle-down” fashion; if a team has a clear best target-earner (usually a WR), he will be fed first regardless of the team’s other receivers. As you move down to secondary and tertiary targets, these players must fight over an increasingly small pie of targets left over from those already spoken for. So, identifying rosters that lack primary target earners and therefore have a large share of targets available to trickle down is generally a winning play at the TE position.

Teams on which the TEs could have a difficult time earning enough targets (due to seeing multiple WRs drafted ahead of them inside the top-60) include the __Cincinnati Bengals__, __Los Angeles Rams__, __Detroit Lions__, and __Dallas Cowboys__. So I’m willing to just cross off __Jake Ferguson__ and __Mike Gesicki__, and any arguments we might make for __Sam LaPorta__ or __Terrance Ferguson__ will need to seriously contend with their need to overcome the receivers ahead of them.

##### …But They Are Usually On Good Offenses

__13 of our 15 league-winning TEs were on offenses that averaged at least 20.0 points per game.__ That isn’t an unreachably high bar — all but six offenses reached it in 2025 — but we should be especially skeptical of TEs on the league’s worst offenses, considering how touchdown-dependent the position is for its fantasy scoring.

One of our best forward-looking signals of offensive quality is Vegas implied team totals, compiled by [Graham Barfield](https://x.com/GrahamBarfield) from lookahead betting lines for the 2026 season. They aren’t perfect predictors, but there was a 0.51 correlation between actual and implied points per game for the 2025 season, making it a strong directional indicator.

__So it’s especially notable to me that three of the current top-six TEs by ADP — Brock Bowers, Trey McBride, and Harold Fannin — are on teams implied for fewer than 20.0 points per game.__ If you’re drafting any of those TEs, you *must* strongly believe in a bull case for their overall offense.

The other teams to whom this applies are the __Miami Dolphins__ and __New York Jets__, while the __New York Giants__, __New Orleans Saints__, __Atlanta Falcons__, __Pittsburgh Steelers__, __Tennessee Titans__, and __Carolina Panthers__ are also in a clear danger zone, implied to score fewer than 22.0 points per game. (Three of the five teams implied for between 20.0 and 22.0 PPG in the 2025 preseason — the Raiders, Titans, and Panthers — ultimately went on to average fewer than 20.0 actual PPG).

This general trend holds for early- and late-round league-winning TEs alike; league-winners from the single-digit rounds saw their teams average 26.2 PPG, while the teams of those from the double-digit rounds averaged 24.5 PPG. For perspective, just 11 teams (roughly a third of the league) averaged more than 24.5 PPG last year; an expected strong offense should be a real bonus to any TE we consider.

Tight End Strategy
------------------

##### Yes, Early-Round TEs Can Work. But Only If They Produce Like The Elite WR1s or RB1s You Could Draft There Instead. Don’t Overthink The Positional Scarcity Angle.

As a reminder (and hey, I originally made this point thousands of words ago, so it’s probably needed), fantasy gamers have had the most relative success with finding league-winning TEs in the late rounds compared to any other position on offense.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/9ab45fa33ebd27ef16886c3d80a1900a4031975b)

Overall, TEs make up just 10.9% of our entire league-winner pool. But that share roughly doubles to 22.7% if we look just in Rounds 10-17.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/0c98681a0037f4c5c51799a61e2aee947ad225c9)

And again, top-3 TEs historically offer just a fraction of the value over replacement player (VORP) vs. the bottom-3 starters at the position compared to at RB and WR.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/aa27d2a5479f04d2da7c0968b71effa7100dac27/46aa24da6e043bf8ee484f532b03e4beb0384d21)

So any TE we might draft in the early rounds — particularly within the first six, where the league-winning hit rates at RB and WR are still materially strong — needs to clear an especially high bar. __And the “positional scarcity” of a top TE doesn’t mean we should grade them on a curve relative to RBs, as points scored by TEs do not create more wins for your fantasy team than points scored by RBs.__

 How many wins are 15-18 fantasy points from an RB worth, compared to starting a replacement-level player? Thanks to @LGilbertFF , we see it's 0.191 wins above replacement (WAR), roughly the same as 15-18 fantasy points from a TE (0.188 WAR). (10-team PPR, 1QB/2RB/2WR/1TE/1FLEX) pic.twitter.com/oU2X1fUOYa — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 22, 2026 

The statements and chart in the tweet above assume a league that mirrors *ESPN’s* default format. If your league instead starts 3 WRs, then fantasy points from the WR position [also become](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2079956758689202321?s=20) just as valuable pound-for-pound as the RB and TE positions, and you should read every mention of RBs over the next three paragraphs as “RBs and WRs.” The analysis doesn’t meaningfully change in 12-team leagues.

The recent successful early-round TEs — Trey McBride in 2025, and Travis Kelce for years before him — largely scored as if they were elite fantasy RB1s. McBride’s 18.6 FPG in 2025 meant he effectively scored as the overall RB6, and he was likewise on a playoff roster in 63% of *ESPN* leagues (would have ranked ~RB4, and within just two percentage points of James Cook, the actual RB6, whom McBride averaged 0.6 more FPG than).

So, consider early-round TEs in terms of the RBs you’re forgoing to select them. If you think one of Brock Bowers or Trey McBride is going to straight-up outscore players like Chase Brown and Derrick Henry (for example) — each of whom go later than both of those TEs on at least one major site — then go ahead and draft them at ADP. But otherwise, you’re probably shooting yourself in the foot. You should pose yourself similar 1v1s for every early TE as you consider whether to draft them.

__Overall, I’m open to drafting a TE early, but only if I’m not in a position to select an RB I believe will outscore him.__ In practice, this means I’m often waiting until ~Round 6-7 or later before seriously considering the position, and the historical success of late-round TE means we shouldn’t be in any real rush.

Tight Ends To Draft Who Could Become League Winners
---------------------------------------------------

As I mentioned above, I’m not fully anti-Brock Bowers this year; I just refuse to select him ahead of RBs like Chase Brown and Derrick Henry, as ADP implies you’ll have to do on several platforms. If Bowers falls to you at the turn or in Round 3 after that RB tier has been wiped off the board, then great. I have an analogous thought process with Colston Loveland.

That probably won’t happen in your draft, though. So here are the potential league-winning TEs that have the best chance of being available in a range I’m comfortable with, after many of our league-winning RBs and WRs are off the board.

##### __Sam LaPorta__, TE, Detroit Lions (*Sleeper ADP: 76.4, TE8*)

LaPorta hits two of our most important league-winning thresholds; he averaged exactly 5.4 targets per game last year, and he’s on a Lions’ offense that leads the NFL in Vegas implied points per game for 2026 (26.4). The only knock on him among our criteria is that, at least according to ADP, this offense is quite *crowded*; both Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams go inside the top-60 (or close enough), and both go ahead of LaPorta.

So, why does LaPorta lead off this list? How do I think he can overcome his target competition?

Well, I’m allowed to simply think that ADP is wrong, aren’t I? The fantasy football hive mind (and, clearly, the ADP market) attributed Jameson Williams’ breakout in the second half of last season to former OC John Morton being stripped of his playcalling duties. But I think it’s at least as likely that Williams just capitalized on LaPorta’s absence, which occurred at roughly the same time.

 Jameson Williams across 8 games with Sam LaPorta inactive: - 7.0 targets/game - 79.4 receiving YPG - 15.1 FPG With LaPorta active: - 4.8 targets/game - 52.7 receiving YPG - 10.9 FPG pic.twitter.com/vY0IcUO5ZG — Fantasy Points Data (@FantasyPtsData) May 12, 2026 

On plays they were on the field together last year, LaPorta commanded a 20.5% target share to Williams’ 17.0%. The gap was even bigger by TPRR (0.21 to 0.16), controlling for the snaps on which LaPorta was blocking. The same is true over their entire careers (LaPorta’s 0.19 to Williams’ 0.18 TPRR when on the field together).

And that’s before we discuss the [impact of](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/new-playcallers-fantasy-football-impact#/) new Lions OC Drew Petzing, who has [flirted with](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/) using more multi-TE sets in some weeks based on matchup (from which LaPorta’s 0.70 FP/RR over the past two seasons ranks 5th-best *among WRs*) and has had Trey McBride run at least a 75% route share in each of his last 29 games in a row. __LaPorta averages 15.9 FPG (~TE2) in 18 career games above a 75% route share__; when he’s been [on the field and healthy](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2054214384126136421?s=20), he’s been quite productive!

 Sam LaPorta in 18 career games above a 75% route share: - 15.9 FPG - 12.9 XFP/G In 24 games below a 75% route share: - 9.8 FPG - 8.1 XFP/G via @FantasyPtsData https://t.co/dTxSYdULdB — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) May 12, 2026 

So LaPorta has multiple paths to nuking this ADP. He could simply turn out to be ahead of Williams in the target pecking order (made more obvious and apparent due to running more routes under Petzing), *or* he could give you strong contingent upside in the event of an injury to either Williams or St. Brown.

##### __George Kittle__, TE, San Francisco 49ers (*Sleeper ADP: 97.4, TE11*)

I didn’t really want to be in on a soon-to-be 33-year-old George Kittle in a season he’s coming off a torn Achilles tendon. The risk is obvious, and the early-season uncertainty will likely [force you](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/biggest-fantasy-injury-questions-of#/) to draft a 2nd TE, costing you a roster spot.

But in a season where every TE is flawed in one way or another according to our league-winning criteria, shouldn’t we regard a relatively cheap Kittle as a gift? He easily clears all the thresholds we’re looking for (6.0 targets per game last year on an offense that ranks 7th-best in Vegas implied PPG and only has Mike Evans sniffing the top-6 rounds of ADP). But more importantly, he’s *George freaking Kittle*, the guy who’s played and produced [through more injuries than Wolverine](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/2010485899939742101?s=20).

Over the past five seasons, Kittle leads all TEs in YPRR (2.41, +19% more than Mark Andrews, the next-closest player). Among all 185 players to see at least 150 targets over the same span, he leads them all in EPA per target (+0.599), ahead of Puka Nacua. Since his sophomore season, Kittle has been a league-winner in both seasons he’s had an *ESPN* ADP of pick 50.0 or later (2019 and 2024); as of this writing, his ADP sits outside the top-80 on that platform, and he’s a fringe top-100 pick on *Sleeper*.

##### __Dalton Kincaid__, TE, Buffalo Bills (*ESPN AD**P: 135.7, TE17*)

This offense is the opposite of crowded — with no pass-catchers being selected inside the first 60 picks (except for DJ Moore on Sleeper, barely) — and it’s incredibly strong, boasting the 6th-most Vegas-implied points per game (25.7). For perspective, four of the five teams above them (Lions, Bengals, Rams, Cowboys) have *multiple* pass-catchers going high. I’m [completely out](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2079201230958592075?s=20) on Moore, so there’s a ton of opportunity here.

Kincaid has one massive and obvious flaw, which I’ve [discussed ad nauseum](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/ryan-heaths-rookie-te-rankings) in my TE evaluations this offseason: due to some combination of injuries and his deficiencies as a blocker, Kincaid didn’t reach a 60% route share a single time last year. (For perspective, each of the top-12 fantasy TEs in 2025 ran a route on at least 66% of their team’s dropbacks over the entire season; 10 of 12 hit at least 74%. Kincaid was at just 44.2%.) We discussed the importance of high-end route volume above, and Kincaid has never had that in his entire career.

But honestly, every TE is flawed in one way or another this year. And I’m as [Toscano-pilled](https://rememberthetightends.substack.com/p/the-true-value-of-a-tight-end-what) as they come, but __Kincaid averaged 14.1 FPG (~TE5) in games he ran over half the routes last year (including playoffs).__ He was so absurdly efficient that he was *almost* fantasy-relevant despite barely playing. __Kincaid averaged 3.19 YPRR; 1.4x that of George Kittle, the most by a TE in__ *__Fantasy Points Data__* __history, and more than any WRs aside from Puka Nacua and Jaxon Smith-Njigba.__

So your evaluation of Kincaid should really come down to the precise combination of injuries and team intention *you* believe explains his playing time last year. And the deeper I look, the more convinced I become that it really was mostly about the injuries, and that the Bills would gladly have Kincaid running 66% or more of the routes if he were healthy.

My evidence? Aside from [everything the Bills’ coaching staff has ever said about him](https://x.com/CoachspeakIndex/status/2080401616352817373?s=20) (TL;DR, they really want Kincaid on the field and were grappling with how to manage his injuries all season), __Kincaid averaged a 65.6% route participation rate in weeks he wasn’t listed on the practice participation report in 2024, or 63.0% over his full career (including postseason).__ Within that same 27-game career split, he averages 5.3 targets per game — right on the edge of our league-winning target volume threshold. And just for fun, if Kincaid had run that 63.0% route share for the Bills at his 2025 efficiency, he’d have amassed nearly 1,200 receiving yards over 17 games, or 15.2 FPG (~TE2).

At his double-digit round cost, I’m completely willing to draft Kincaid, see what happens in Week 1, and jump ship immediately if he runs a sub-50% route share. I just think there’s a real chance the industry has massively overthought this one. Maybe he pulls his hamstring in the preseason, and this never matters, but I can’t get the thought of a surprise top-5 fantasy season from Kincaid out of my head.

##### __Oronde Gadsden__, TE, Los Angeles Chargers (*ESPN ADP: 168.2, TE23*)

Gadsden hits on every league-winning breakout indicator. He’s in a Chargers’ offense that lacks early-ADP pass-catchers outside of Ladd McConkey, ranks in the top half of the NFL in implied points per game (23.6, which I’d even argue significantly undersells them), and is entering Year 2. That’s 3-for-3!

But just like in Kincaid’s case, the primary question with Gadsden is simply whether he’ll play enough to be fantasy-relevant, especially in light of the Chargers signing both Charlie Kolar (a capable inline blocker, unlike Gadsden) and David Njoku. I argued [here](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/) that this is the wrong way to think about the question; on a team with no established third receiver that just had their TEs and the departed Keenan Allen combine for over 250 slot routes on early downs alone, why couldn’t Gadsden simply play as the de facto slot on 1st and 2nd down, and inline on obvious passing downs?

It’s at least possible, especially considering that under new Chargers OC Mike McDaniel, fellow “bad inline blocker” TEs Darren Waller (post-rap career at age 33) and Jonnu Smith (having his first truly fantasy-relevant season in Year 8) have averaged 14.5 FPG (~TE5) over their last 17 non-injured games. *__That’s all despite Smith and Waller having exceeded a 70% route share only three times.__* Gadsden himself literally did that five times last year!

Again, I’m completely okay with eating crow and telling you to drop Gadsden if he only runs 5-10 routes in Week 1. I acknowledge that’s a real possibility. But at a position with few real difference-makers and for the price of “basically free,” I’m willing to take the upside swing on one of the most [productive college TEs of the past several draft classes](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2025/scott-barretts-analytics-darlings-tes) that averaged 16.5 FPG in the four games he did play a full-time (75%+ route share) role as a rookie.

Kickers And Defenses
--------------------

Referring again to the data at the top of this article, defenses and kickers offer roughly one-half and one-fourth the value of QBs/TEs, respectively. Moreover, the rare league-winners at these positions have historically been available within the final rounds of drafts; we are [worse at predicting them](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1549096955808301060) than all other positions. The floor from streaming them (playing a different D/ST or K each week based on matchup) is also historically quite high.

I wrote detailed articles on how to draft and stream these positions ([Defenses](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2023/how-to-draft-and-stream-fantasy-defenses#/), [Kickers](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2023/how-to-draft-and-stream-fantasy-kickers#/)) back in 2023, and the broad advice within them on how to evaluate the positions still applies today. Feel free to read them if you’re interested.

__The only thing I’d add here is that if your draft doesn’t take place immediately before Week 1 kicks off and your league’s rules allow it, I’d entirely forgo selecting a kicker or D/ST.__ These players cannot gain value between the preseason and Week 1, but a team’s RB2 (for example) absolutely can, in the event the starter gets injured in training camp or a preseason game. This is a micro-edge that may only pay off over many leagues and seasons of playing fantasy football. But why not give yourself the chance to hold a player like James Conner in the year of Le’Veon Bell’s surprise holdout? If that doesn’t happen, you can simply drop these players to add a kicker and defense immediately before Week 1.

TL;DR (Overall Draft Strategy)
------------------------------

+ __Unless you can select Jalen Hurts with all your RB/WR/FLEX spots already filled, draft whichever of Trevor Lawrence or Justin Herbert falls to ~Round 10. If neither does, take 1-2 of the several late-round QBs with rushing upside and/or who plays in a McShanahan offense (Kyler Murray, Malik Willis, Baker Mayfield, etc.)__

+ __Draft at least one RB (preferably two) through the first two rounds, and at least two (preferably three) through the first six. Avoid the RB dead zone beginning in Rounds 3-4 (specifically, Breece Hall, Kyren Williams, Javonte Williams, Travis Etienne).__

+ __Draft 4-5 WRs before the cliff hits in Round 10, keeping in mind that it may be harder to find useful WRs in the late rounds than ever before.__

+ __Don’t draft a TE early if it means foregoing an RB you believe will outscore him. Depending on the players, I’m open to taking two late shots at the position.__

+ __Wait until the final two rounds to draft a kicker and defense, or don’t draft one at all.__

Again, all of this is based on *ESPN’s* default settings: a 10-team PPR league that starts 1 QB, 2 RBs, 2 WRs, 1 TE, and 1 FLEX.

In leagues with 12+ teams, leagues with a 3rd WR spot, or leagues with an additional FLEX spot (or any combination of the three), WRs become more important. However, the broad player archetypes you should be targeting (discussed throughout this article) all still apply.

full_text:
I’m changing the format of my annual fantasy football Draft Plan article this year and have decided to separate my actual plan from the detailed write-ups I do on my key player targets. I don’t think the Draft Plan article will suffer at all, since I’ll be naming all the players I’m targeting in the article, as usual. I just think the article got too large and cumbersome, so I’ll be publishing (and constantly updating) my entire player target list with analysis in this new “Guru’s Guys” article.

Make no mistake: while the Draft Plan is critical, I view my player targets as the most important part of the plan, and therefore the most important thing I do in the preseason. In the past, I’ve isolated about 70 of the top 300 players for my target list, but I’m getting even more selective with age. Lately, I’ve narrowed the list down to 50 players, or only 25% of the top-200 players. In a typical 12-team league, 216 players will be drafted, so my select group of 50 players represents 23% of the 2026 player pool.

Before I get into the players, here’s a checklist of my criteria, so you know exactly what I’m looking for in my player targets:

1.  __Value__ — To break it down in its most basic form, I’m mostly looking for players who I believe will outproduce their draft positions (ADP). The more expensive a player is, the harder it is for him to make it onto my list. I generally do not include consensus top-12 overall picks on my list of player targets.

+   __Production and role__ — For players I think are appropriately priced, I need to be confident in their ability to produce and their volume/role. For RBs, versatility is a huge factor. For pass-catchers, things like target share, first-read target share, etc., are hugely important, and scheme also matters here.
+   __Infrastructure__ — Ideally, a player target of mine is in a stable organization. I’m looking for continuity with positive coaching and play-calling in a proven system with a strong supporting cast (especially a quality offensive line).
+   __Age and durability__ — I greatly value youth and tend to be ageist, but I will make some exceptions when an older player is generally durable and relatively affordable.

As you can see, my standards are high. With only 32 players out of 200 on my list this year, I’m weeding out over 85% of the player pool, so a player needs to check a lot of positive boxes for me to back him. __I’ll surely add some more players to my list in August, but I’m hoping my selectivity leads to better accuracy.__

\> *__Note__**: I’m listing the players in order of ADP, but I’ll also rank the players based on my ideal order of preference below.*

### __Players removed since last update:__

+   __Ricky Pearsall__ (WR, SF) — Welp, I banned him from “The 12” list in my [Draft Plan](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2026/the-gurus-fantasy-draft-plan) due to his serious availability issues, and I’m glad I did. His health status was unclear until very recently but now there’s word that his entire season may be in jeopardy, so he’s off my list.

### __Guru’s Top 2026 Quarterback Targets__

__{{Justin Herbert|QB|LAC|21681}}__ (LAC, 85) — While they don’t run off a ton of plays, the __Jim Harbaugh__/__Mike McDaniel__ marriage should be magical, especially with their excellent OTs back and healthy. In 2022, __Tua Tagovailoa__, with noticeable limitations and all, led the NFL in TD percentage (6.3%) and YPA (8.9), and in 2023, he led in passing yards (4624) under McDaniel. The selection of speedy WR __Brenen Thompson__ could give them the lid-lifter they’ve lacked and complete their (already solid) receiving corps. LA also added veteran TE __David Njoku__, giving Herbert a fully-stocked receiving corps with 6-7 strong options. Herbert last year was tied for 5th in rushing attempts (83) and second in rushing yards (498) last year, so I think we can count on top-7 rushing production with the offense in the hands of two strong offensive minds who are run-oriented. He played behind a decimated OL all season, so Herbert was only 17th in FP/DB, yet he was also still 7th in catchable throw percentage. He’s only the eighth or ninth QB off the board this summer, but with better health around him this year, he should slice and dice NFL defenses, continue to rush the ball 5-6 times a game, and post top-7 fantasy digits.

{{PAYWALL}}

__{{Trevor Lawrence|QB|JAX|22490}}__ (Jax, 89) — Lawrence’s ADP of QB11 is beyond reasonable for a player who looked like the best QB in the league down the stretch and who ranked *first* in FPG (23.5) the final 10 weeks of 2025. Lawrence’s YPA and completion rates were identical to the year before, so his production was boosted by his 9 TDs on the ground (7 in the final 10 weeks). But he scattered 12 rushing TDs over his previous three seasons, and the ground production should continue in an improved offense that was 6th in Points For under new HC __Liam Coen__. Lawrence looked more comfortable than ever under Coen, especially after Coen simplified the offense and advised his QB to “let it rip” in a Week 10 pep talk, which he did. He’ll likely need to keep running in TDs to give you spike weeks, but this offense is likely still ascending with a full year of __Jakobi Meyers__ and with __Brian Thomas__ seemingly incapable of playing as poorly as he did last year. Lawrence had the second-highest drop percentage in the league (8.6%) and the most dropped yards (397), per FP Data, but the vibes have been great on Thomas, Meyers, __Parker Washington__, and the recently-extended TE __Brenton Strange__. But it was a nightmarish and volatile year that ended in a late-season torn ACL, so he was basically off my radar last summer. But immediately upon his return last season, I was fairly stunned by his improved hands and physicality at the catch point, and he posted the best catch rate of his career (63.3%) while maintaining a high 17.5 YPR average. He was truly “commanding the ball” in this offense, which is saying something, given the Packers had a plethora of strong receiving options, and he produced against man coverage (2.55 YPRR) and zone coverage (2.87). There are two fewer options now with __Romeo Doubs__ and __Dontayvion Wicks__ off the roster, and I get the sense that HC __Matt LaFleur__ is finally ready to actually feature his best receivers, namely Watson, who is, by far, their best option at the “X” receiver spot. Watson won’t likely be a high-volume receiver on the 2026 Packers, but he was only 51st in the NFL last season in targets-per-routes-run, so his volume is set to rise on a thinned-out Packers’ receiving corps. Watson has scored 20 TDs on only 133 career receptions, which is an excellent 15% TD rate, and it’s up to 17% if we remove his injury-plagued 2024 campaign. A WR1 season may be inevitable if he can avoid injury.

__{{Michael Pittman|WR|PIT}}__ (Pit, 99) — I’ve been a __D.K. Metcalf__ hater from Day One, and I was a big Pittman guy coming out, so I’m naturally favoring the former Colt this year over the former Seahawk. Metcalf used to crush man coverage, but in 2025, his 1.46 YPPR against man was only 43rd out of 76 WRs with at least 50 targets. Meanwhile, his 2.40 YPPR against zone was 16th-best last year. The problem is, Metcalf is going to get more downfield looks this year, and that’s a problem with __Aaron Rodgers__, who was 59th (!!) at QB last year with a 6.2 aDOT, and he was 46th at QB in deep throw percentage (9.4%). So basically, with 40% of their 2025 targets gone (third most), I expect Pittman, who saw about 90% of his targets in the short/intermediate area, to be their volume receiver. I’ve interacted with Pittman several times and he’s an old soul whose father played in the league with Rodgers, so I’m very confident that Rodgers will love him.

__{{Josh Downs|WR|IND|24145}}__ (Ind, 114) — Injuries are definitely a concern for the diminutive Downs, who has dealt with thigh, hamstring, shoulder, toe, ankle, and knee issues in the NFL. But balancing the upside if he can enjoy improved health along with his downside if injuries persist, I think he’s a good pick. Downs ran only 18.5% of his routes from the outside last season, but __Michael Pittman__ and his 345 outside routes are gone (as is __A.D. Mitchell__, who was traded after playing eight games with the Colts last year). Indy signed veteran __Nick Westbrook-Ikhine__, but he’s more of a downfield specialist, and Downs is the more skilled receiver, so unless they sign a guy like __Keenan Allen__, Downs is expected to soak up some of the reps outside in 12 personnel, which is a big development for the usually slot-centric receiver. A bigger development might be wideout __Alec Pierce__ landing on PUP and looking iffy to open the season. That’s another critical factor with Downs, so his ADP is likely to rise. But I highly doubt it’ll rise to a point at which I’m no longer in. __UPDATED__: 7/30

__{{Alec Pierce|WR|IND|23232}}__ (Ind, 67 — PROJECTED TO 115 BY MID-AUG) — With the Colts letting __Michael Pittman__ go and signing Pierce to a four-year contract extension worth up to $116 million, I’m surprised Pierce isn’t getting a little more love (a March ankle surgery to clean up a two-year issue is likely the reason). Most know about his downfield acumen, as Pierce ended the season first in aDOT (19.4), YPR (21.34), and YPT (11.94), and fourth in air yards share (43%) among 76 WRs who saw 50+ targets, and he’s averaged a ridiculous 18.7 YPR through his first four seasons. But he showed a more complete skill set in his fourth season, and the Colts clearly believe that his game will continue to expand with more volume. He has ideal size at 6’3”, 211 pounds, and his hands are excellent, which helps him in contested catch situations. The problem as of late July is that he opened camp on the PUP list, and [our resident doctor is a little concerned](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/league-winners-targets-and-values#/h.running-backs). He’s definitely in line to get off to a slow start, but his ADP is going to rise, so I’ll keep him on my list for now (but will also drop him to the bottom of my Hansen 50 list below). __UPDATED__: 7/30

__{{Xavier Worthy|WR|KC|24924}}__ (KC, 122) — Worthy has never made my list before, and I think he has some problems (lack of size, ball tracking), but I’m interested in buying this season. That’s based on their need at receiver, the OC change, and his depressed cost. It’s also worth noting that __Patrick Mahomes__ (knee) was cleared for the opening of camp, as was Worthy (shoulder). I simply think Worthy may be ready to show us the best he has to offer — whatever that is — in year three, and I do think a recommitment to running the ball will open up some downfield opportunities. __ADDED__: 7/30

__{{Jalen Coker|WR|CAR|25122}}__ (Car, 136) — The former undrafted rookie had a mini breakout back in 2024, but I wasn’t buying into him playing on a team with __Bryce Young__ starting at QB that year. His upside is still likely capped by Young, but Coker was impressive down the stretch in 2025, and I did buy into his emergence. He was awesome in their playoff loss when he posted 9/134/1 on 12 targets, and the Panthers are clearly into him, since they recently extended him with a three-year deal that will keep him around through the 2029 season. Rookie WR __Chris Brazzell’s__ season is already over due to a knee injury, so Coker looks like the clear #2 WR. That’s over __Xavier Legette__, who has more targets per game and per route run than Coker last year. Per Fantasy Points Data, Coker was 7th in EPA (expected points added) per route year, and more routes this year mean he has easy top-40 potential, even on this team. He’s at worst a small value as about the WR 50-55 off the board this summer. __ADDED__: 7/30

__{{Jalen McMillan|WR|TB|25098}}__ (TB, 160) — Of all the people on my initial list this year, I can see McMillan making the biggest leap in terms of ADP come August. But even if his stock rises 3-4 full rounds, I still think he’s a value. McMillan really flashed as a rookie with 8 TDs on only 58 targets, and while his sophomore season was ruined by a serious neck issue, he managed to catch 12 of 15 targets (80% catch rate) while averaging a healthy 14.5 YPR and leading the team with 2.41 YPPR. With Mike Evans off the roster, McMillon will likely play mostly outside, where he lined up 78% of the time last year, but he does have strong inside-outside versatility. He’s clicked well with Baker Mayfield, so I would not be shocked if McMillan winds up being their second-leading receiver — or even number one.

__{{Jerry Jeudy|WR|CLE|21692}}__ (Cle, 160) — I’m mostly avoiding Browns players this year, but I’m too into ROI opportunities to ignore the fact that Jeudy looks like a great flyer in the 13th or 14th round. They drafted two promising wideouts this past spring, but Jeudy is the incumbent No. 1 receiver, and the veteran is still only 27 years old. With an unsettled QB situation it’s going to be more difficult for rookies __KC Concepcion__ and __Denzel Boston__ to assimilate quickly, so leaning on the veteran Jeudy makes a lot of sense. Jeudy is signed through the 2027 season, but if one of both of the rookies are kicking ass earlier in the season, Jeudy would be a great player for the Browns to trade. If he’s moved, it’ll likely be a QB and situational upgrade. __ADDED__: 7/30

__{{Jalen Nailor|WR|LV|23368}}__ (LV, 167) — Veteran __Tre Tucker__ looks like a value in his own right, but the new staff did hand pick Nailor in free agency this year, and he played with __Kirk Cousins__ in Minnesota running a similar offense, so I think he has more upside than the markets recognize. He was the Vikings’ “man-beater” last year with excellent numbers against the coverage, and per Fantasy Points Data, Nailor was the third-best separator by average separation score when lined up out-wide last year. If he can excel inside and outside, he has a great chance to emerge as their “No. 1” WR. __ADDED__: 7/30

__{{Deebo Samuel|WR|FA|20932}}__ (FA, 171) — I’ve been a big Deebo guy from Day 1, and I even had him as one of my top-12 targets last year, and he crushed his ADP with a WR25 finish overall on the season. Wherever he lands, it’ll likely be in an offense that both needs him and is able to utilize him. __ADDED__: 7/30

__{{Calvin Ridley|WR|TEN|19802}}__ (Ten, 200) — I liked him as a 7th-rounder last year, and it went horribly, but the offense should improve considerably with a new OC and some experience for his QB, and Ridley is now properly cast as a #2, so he might log one more solid season. __ADDED__: 7/30

### __Guru’s Top 2026 Tight End Targets__

__{{Brock Bowers|TE|LV|24943}}__ (LV, 21) — The timing looks ideal for Bowers to return great value as a 2nd-round fantasy pick, since he’s coming off an injury-marred season that was also disrupted majorly due to poor QB play and a horrible offense. In theory, all three negatives have been resolved, since Bowers is expected to be 100% and ready to go for training camp. He also now has a dynamic offensive mind running the show in new HC __Klint Kubiak__, who has called Bowers a “football robot from heaven.” And finally, between QBs __Kirk Cousins__ and __Fernando Mendoza__, not to mention a prized FA pickup in C __Tyler Linderbaum__, the overall competence of the offense should rise considerably. The Raiders are high on former Viking __Jalen Nailor__, and he is a viable “sleeper” this year, but make no mistake: the passing game will go through Bowers, who will likely draw a huge contract extension at season’s end if he has a big year. With an ADP around 20, fantasy managers can select a stud RB or WR in Round 1, add Bowers in Round 2, and still likely get an excellent asset early in Round 3.

__{{Tyler Warren|TE|IND|25874}}__ (Ind, 60) — Warren, as a rookie last year, was fifth in route share (79.9%), third in targets (106), and sixth in target-per-game (6.2) and target share (19.4%) — and now veteran __Michael Pittman__ and his 19.7% target share last year is off the roster. Pittman will be replaced by __Nick Westbrook-Ikhine__, who’s never had more than 38 catches in a season, so I think it’s fair to expect Warren’s usage to increase in year two. Warren was only 21st in the team's TD percentage, and a little TD love, along with minimal time missed, should result in an elite season. If __Daniel Jones__ is able to play in 14+ games, then Warren looks like a league-winner at his 5th round ADP. Even if the Alec Pierce situation elevates Warren squarely in the fourth round, I’m still in. __UPDATED__: 7/30

__{{Tucker Kraft|TE|GB|24118}}__ (GB, 76) — With veterans __Romeo Doubs__ and __Dontavian Wicks__ off the roster, that leaves a 28.5% target share open and up for grabs in Green Bay, which is notable because Kraft was only 14th in TE target percentage and only 18th at his position with a 69.3% route share. Even worse, he was only 23rd at TE with .22 TPRR last year. His QB __Jordan Love__ trusts him majorly, which is notable because his volume is increasing this year for sure. Among 54 TEs with at least 25 targets, Kraft was second with .62 FP/RR, and he was third at the position with a stellar 2.54 YPRR, so his potential is blatantly obvious. As of 7/30, Kraft was still on PUP, but the expectation was that he could come off at any time, so he seems fully on track for Week 1. __UPDATED__: 7/30

__{{Sam LaPorta|TE|DET|23141}}__ (Det, 91) — LaPorta is coming off an injury-marred season, but considering his high-end ability and a limited target tree in Detroit, he could be the best TE value on the board this year. In 2025, __Jameson Williams__ averaged 7.0 targets, 79.4 receiving yards, and 15.1 FPG in eight games with LaPorta inactive. But with LaPorta active, Jamo saw only 4.8 targets, 52.7 receiving yards, and 10.9 FPG, so LaPorta may simply need to be available to come through. If healthy, he should match his 76.8% route share from ‘25, since the Lions have added only veteran slot receiver __Greg Dortch__ this offseason (and they lost veteran slot receiver __Kalif Raymond__). And in 18 career games with a route share of 75% or higher, LaPorta has averaged 15.9 FPG, which would have been good for TE2 in FPG last season. Last year, among TEs with 200+ routes run, Laporta was top-2 in: YPT, YPRR, and YAC/per. They’ve lost some players on defense along with some juice in the backfield with __David Montgomery__ gone, so we should get a slight uptick in terms of pass attempts. LaPorta should clearly be the third option in the passing game, and he is due for some scoring regression, since his 11.6% TD rate from 2023-2024 was down to only 7.5% last year.

__{{Travis Kelce|TE|KC|15048}}__ (KC, 110) — I’m usually out on old heads, but Kelce was on my list last year, and despite the __Patrick Mahomes__ injury that left the team with a hopeless situation at QB, Kelce was still the TE3 in total scoring and the TE9 in FPG (11.4 FPG). However, if you exclude Weeks 16, 17, and 18 without Mahomes, Kelce was his usual elite self with 12.8 FPG, which was good for TE5 in FPG. There will be a newfound affinity for the running game with OC __Eric Bieniemy__ back in the building, but Kelce is thrilled that he’s back, and there’s usually a connection between a commitment to the run and TE production. Hell, for all we know, Kelce may have retired if he had to deal with __Matt Nagy__ again, so I see no reason why Kelce can’t have yet another strong season at 37 years old, which is exactly what fellow all-time great __Tony Gonzalez__ did in his final season (83/859/8). For what it’s worth, Kelce is reportedly off to a nice start in camp.

__{{Jake Ferguson|TE|DAL|23138}}__ (DAL, 112) — Intriguing young WR __Ryan Flournoy__ played well last year, but Ferguson still looks like the third option in the passing game in Dallas. There’s excellent continuity in Dallas with HC __Brian Schottenheimer__ entering year two and 10-year starter __Dak Prescott__ working behind an OL that is returning all five starters, including three Round 1 selections. And if George Pickens has any problems playing under the franchise tag, then the team’s reliance on Ferguson will increase.

__{{Mark Andrews|TE|BAL|19803}}__ (Bal, 121) — It’s fair to say that Andrews is slowing down, and his Average Separation Scores declined in 2025 compared to 2024. Of course, Baltimore also lost TEs __Isaiah Likely__ and __Charlie Kolar__ and will try to break in a pair of rookie TEs drafted in the fourth and fifth rounds with veteran blocking TE __Durham Smythe__ (4 receptions in 17 games last year in Chicago) in line to play a lot this year. Andrews ran 70% of his routes from the slot last season, and his Average Separation Score was still ninth-best among 69 TEs with 100 routes, while his Win Rate was seventh-best, better than __Kyle Pitts__, __Colston Loveland__, and __Trey McBride__. He’ll be 31 in September, and there is a potential out in his contract after 2026, but the club signed him to a three-year, $39.3 million contract extension this past December with over $20 million guaranteed, so they’re counting on him majorly at least this year. And since they’ll be working two rookie wideouts in a weakened receiving corps this year, __Lamar Jackson__ should be counting on his boy Andrews to be his security blanket.

__{{Brenton Strange|TE|JAX|24223}}__ (Jax, 139) — As the TE18 off the board, Strange was my “sleeper TE” pick for 2025, and if we remove his Week 5 game in which he was injured and played only 38% of the snaps (1 catch for 22 yards), he was the TE7 in total scoring and the TE11 in FPG in the 11 games he played in. He was eighth in catches (45) and fifth in receiving yards (518) with a higher YPR average than luminaries like __Harold Fannin__, __Tyler Warren__, and __Brock Bowers__. There’s a lot of hype about WRs __Brian Thomas__, __Jakobi Meyers__, and __Parker Washington__ this year and rightfully so, but the Jags just gave him a fat contract extension in June, and Trevor loves him, so I still see Strange as being sneaky-productive.

__{{Greg Dulcich|TE|MIA|23310}}__ (Mia, 225) — Athletic and still young, he looks poised to settle in as a top-2 target for __Malik Willis__, so the potential ROI is too good to pass up after he finished SECOND in YPRR last year among 139 qualifying TEs at 2.64. Dulcich reportedly clicked well with Willis in the OTAs, and he’s been flying around like a gazelle early in camp, so now it’s just a question of how far does the hype train go this summer? Regardless, I’ve been a passenger on that train from Day 1.
